questions.q: Where does MySQL's LIMIT clause go, compared to T-SQL's TOP?
options: LIMIT goes at the end of the query; TOP goes right after SELECT
LIMIT goes right after SELECT, exactly where TOP does
LIMIT goes before the FROM clause
LIMIT and TOP are both placed after GROUP BY only
questions.explain: This is a structural difference, not just a renamed keyword — LIMIT belongs at the end of the statement.

questions.q: What replaces T-SQL's + operator for string concatenation in MySQL?
options: CONCAT()
+ works identically in MySQL
STRING_AGG()
The || operator
questions.explain: MySQL reserves + for arithmetic only, so string concatenation requires the explicit CONCAT() function.

questions.q: What replaces T-SQL's CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) numeric style-code date formatting in MySQL?
options: DATE_FORMAT(date, format_string) using %m/%d/%Y-style tokens
CONVERT works identically with the same style codes in MySQL
CAST(date AS VARCHAR) with no format control
TO_CHAR(date, 'MM/DD/YYYY')
questions.explain: MySQL has no numeric style-code convention like T-SQL's CONVERT — DATE_FORMAT uses its own token-based format strings.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, did the WITH (CTE) syntax itself need to change when translating to MySQL?
options: No — WITH is standard SQL and needed no change; only the dialect-specific pieces inside it did
Yes — MySQL requires WITH RECURSIVE for every CTE, even non-recursive ones
Yes — MySQL does not support CTEs at all
Yes — MySQL requires CTEs to be written as subqueries instead
questions.explain: The CTE syntax itself is standard SQL; only TOP, +, and CONVERT needed MySQL-specific replacements.

questions.q: What is the general pattern this lesson demonstrates about cross-dialect translation?
options: Most of a query translates untouched; the real work is spotting the handful of vendor-specific pieces
Every single clause in a query must be rewritten from scratch for each dialect
T-SQL and MySQL share no syntax in common at all
Translation is impossible without a dedicated migration tool
questions.explain: This chapter's queries show that standard SQL (SELECT/FROM/WHERE/CTEs) carries over directly — only specific functions and clauses need swapping.
